title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about referencing at university: what it is, why it matters, and how to do it accurately. By the end you will be able to explain what referencing is and why it matters, recognise the main referencing styles and what a reference is made of, and reference your sources accurately when you quote and when you paraphrase.

Referencing is not a box-ticking chore added at the end of an essay. 'Reference your sources' is one of the first instructions you meet at university, and getting it right credits the people whose ideas you use, shows a tutor the reading behind your work, and keeps you on the right side of academic integrity. It affects how your work reads and the marks it earns.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what referencing is and why it matters at university
recognise the main referencing styles and what a reference is made of
reference sources accurately when you quote and when you paraphrase.

title: In real academic practice
body: Referencing is a habit academic work is built on. Every essay that draws on reading, every report that cites evidence, every piece of work where you use someone else's idea, relies on acknowledging where that idea came from. Build the habit now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the professional work that later expects you to credit your sources and evidence your claims.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what referencing is and why it matters: the purpose behind the practice. Second, referencing styles and the parts of a reference: the main styles and what every reference is built from. Third, referencing accurately: how to acknowledge a source when you quote and when you paraphrase. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: When you are told to 'reference your sources', it can sound like a rule to follow rather than something that matters. It is easy to treat it as a chore added at the end, or as nothing more than a way of not getting caught for plagiarism. Referencing is more than that: it is how you acknowledge where the knowledge in your work comes from. This lesson looks at what referencing is and why it matters, so the instruction stops being a chore and starts making sense.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and referencing may be new as something you do deliberately. At this stage you are not expected to have memorised a style guide. The aim is to understand what referencing is and why it matters - the purpose behind it - which is the foundation you will build the practical habit on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that referencing means acknowledging where the knowledge in your work comes from
recognise, in a worked example, why references matter beyond simply avoiding plagiarism
identify what a reference list shows a tutor about a piece of work in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Referencing is the practice of acknowledging where the knowledge you use in your work comes from. When you draw on someone else's idea, theory, finding or words, a reference records whose it was and where you found it, so that a reader can tell what is yours and what you have borrowed, and can trace it back to the original.

It is tempting to think referencing is only about avoiding plagiarism, but it does much more than that. Crediting an idea to its author is part of academic integrity: presenting someone else's idea as your own is dishonest, whether or not you meant it. References also show a tutor the scope of your reading, and they let you evidence your work against the marking criteria. Many tutors look at the reference list first, to get a sense of the research behind a piece of work.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last piece of work you handed in. Did you reference your sources as you went, or add them at the end as a chore? What difference might it make to treat referencing as crediting the people whose ideas you used?

title: Summary
body: Referencing is how you acknowledge where the knowledge in your work comes from, not a chore bolted on at the end. You can now explain what referencing is and say why it matters: it credits the people whose ideas you use, it is part of academic integrity, and it shows a tutor the scope of your reading. The next lessons turn this purpose into practice - the styles and parts of a reference, and how to reference accurately when you quote and paraphrase.

_items.title: See pages 188 and 191 to 193 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw what referencing is and why it matters. This lesson is about the forms it takes. Referencing comes in more than one style, and whichever one you use, every reference is built from the same handful of parts. Knowing the styles and the parts means a reference stops looking like a jumble of names, dates and italics and starts making sense.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to memorise a style guide or to format every kind of source perfectly. The aim here is to recognise that different disciplines use different styles, and to see the parts that every reference is made from, so you know what you are looking at and what a reference needs to contain.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise that there are several referencing styles and that different disciplines use different ones
identify the parts a reference is built from (author, date, title and the conventions that format them)
recognise which referencing style is commonly used in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Referencing has no single correct layout. Author-date styles such as Harvard (used widely across many disciplines) and APA (common in psychology and the social sciences) are among the most common. Others include MHRA and Chicago (often used in the humanities), Vancouver (medical and clinical subjects), IEEE (engineering and computing) and OSCOLA (law). Your department will tell you which style to use; the important thing is to use one style and use it consistently.

Whatever the style, a reference is built from the same parts: who wrote it (the author), when it was published (the date), what it is called (the title), and where it can be found (the publication details). The conventions differ - the author's surname comes first, followed by their initial, and the title of a book is set in italics - but once you can see these parts, you can read and build a reference in any style.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Find out which referencing style your own subject uses. Look at a reference in it: can you pick out the author, the date, the title and the publication details?

title: Summary
body: Several referencing styles exist - Harvard, APA, MHRA, Vancouver and others - and different disciplines use different ones, so your department will tell you which to use. Underneath the differences, every reference is built from the same parts: author, date, title and publication details, arranged by the conventions of the style. You can now recognise the main styles, identify the parts of a reference, and say which style your own subject is likely to use. The next lesson is about using them accurately when you quote and paraphrase.

_items.title: See pages 188 to 191 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You have seen what referencing is, why it matters, and the forms a reference takes. This lesson is about doing it accurately. Two things trip students up most often: not realising that paraphrasing needs a reference just as quoting does, and letting small errors creep into the references themselves. This lesson deals with both.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to produce a flawless reference list from memory. The aim is to know when a reference is needed - when you quote and when you paraphrase - and to recognise the difference between an accurate reference and one with errors, so you can check your own work.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that you need an in-text reference both when you quote and when you paraphrase
tell an accurate reference apart from one with errors or inconsistencies
choose the accurate way to reference a quotation or a paraphrase in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
You need an in-text reference whenever you use someone else's idea, and that is true in two cases that are easy to confuse. When you quote, you use an author's exact words, inside quotation marks, with a reference. When you paraphrase, you put their idea into your own words - but it is still their idea, so it still needs a reference. A paraphrase without a reference presents someone else's thinking as your own, which is exactly what referencing exists to prevent.

Accuracy matters as much as acknowledgement. A reference that muddles the author, the date or the title, or that is formatted inconsistently, is harder for a reader to trust and to follow. It is tempting to copy a ready-made reference from your library's discovery service or a PDF, but this is where inaccuracies and inconsistencies creep in. Build your references from the parts yourself, and check them against the style your department uses.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a time you put an author's idea into your own words. Did you add a reference? After this lesson, would you reference it differently?

title: Summary
body: Referencing accurately comes down to two habits: reference whenever you use someone else's idea - when you paraphrase as well as when you quote - and set each reference out carefully and consistently, rather than pasting in a ready-made one that may carry errors. You can now explain when an in-text reference is needed, tell an accurate reference from a flawed one, and choose the accurate way to reference a quotation or a paraphrase. With the purpose, the parts and the practice in place, you are ready to reference your own work with confidence.

_items.title: See pages 193 to 198 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Referencing is no longer a vague chore: it is a practice you understand and can carry out. You can explain what referencing is - acknowledging where the knowledge in your work comes from - and why it matters, from crediting authors and academic integrity to showing a tutor the scope of your reading. title: In real academic practice
body: From here, referencing is something you practise in every module. Each time you draw on a reading, quote a source or paraphrase an idea, the habit is at work. It is also what academic and professional life rewards: crediting your sources and evidencing your claims accurately builds the trust that serious work depends on, well beyond your degree.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What referencing really is
body: Four common ideas about referencing that miss the point. Turn each card to see what referencing is really for.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: Referencing is often taught as a way to avoid being accused of plagiarism. That is part of it, but the real point is positive: you are crediting the people whose ideas you use and showing the reading behind your work.

front.title: Not a chore for the end

back.body: Referencing is not a tidy-up job bolted on after the writing is done. The ideas you borrow are part of the argument as you build it, so recording where they came from belongs in the work from the start.

When you use someone's idea, theory or finding, a reference says whose it was. Presenting their thinking as your own, even by accident, is dishonest; a reference keeps the line between your ideas and theirs clear.
A reference list tells a reader how widely and how carefully you have read. Many tutors look at it first, because it signals the scope and quality of the research behind a piece of work.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The main referencing styles
body: Four families of referencing style. Select each tab to see where it is used and what marks it out.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that style.

_items.title: Harvard (author-date)
_items.body: An author-date style: the author's surname and the year appear in the text, like (Dennis, 2026), with the full details in the reference list. Harvard is used widely across many disciplines, which is why it is often the first style students meet.

_items.title: APA (author-date)
_items.body: Another author-date style, set by the American Psychological Association. It is the standard in psychology and much of the social sciences, and in business-related subjects. It looks similar to Harvard but has its own rules for punctuation and layout.

_items.title: MHRA and Chicago
_items.body: Humanities subjects often use footnote styles such as MHRA or Chicago, where a small number in the text points to a note at the foot of the page or end of the chapter. These suit writing that discusses sources closely.

_items.title: Vancouver, IEEE and OSCOLA
_items.body: Some fields use numbered styles: Vancouver in medical and clinical subjects, IEEE in engineering and computing, and OSCOLA in law. A number in the text matches a numbered entry in the list. Your department will tell you which to use.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Referencing accurately
body: Four moves that keep your referencing accurate. Select each heading to reveal the move.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Reference the paraphrase too
_items.body: It is easy to think only direct quotes need a reference. They do, but so does a paraphrase: the words are yours, the idea is still the author's, so it needs crediting just as a quotation does.

_items.title: Quote exactly, mark it clearly
_items.body: When you use an author's exact words, put them in quotation marks and give a reference with the page. A quotation that is not marked as one reads as if the words were yours.

_items.title: Build the reference from its parts
_items.body: Rather than pasting a ready-made reference from a discovery service or PDF, put it together yourself from the author, date, title and publication details. That is how you catch errors and keep to one style.

_items.title: Check for consistency
_items.body: Accuracy is also about consistency: the same style, punctuation and order throughout. A list that mixes styles or muddles the parts is harder for a reader to trust and to follow.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two students using the same book chapter in an essay.

{{learner-a}} uses the chapter's idea in the essay and, at the end, adds it to a reference list so as not to be accused of copying. The source is listed, but {{learner-a}} thinks of referencing only as a way of staying out of trouble, added once the writing is done. Whether the idea is clearly credited where it is used, or whether the list shows the reading behind the work, has not really been considered. This treats referencing as a chore.

{{learner-b}} references the same chapter as the idea is used, naming the author in the text and giving the full details in the list. For {{learner-b}}, the reference credits the author whose idea this is, keeps the line between borrowed and original thinking clear, and shows the tutor the reading behind the argument. Avoiding plagiarism follows from this, rather than being the whole point.

Both students listed the source. Only {{learner-b}} used referencing for what it is really for: crediting ideas and evidencing research.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students need to reference the same book chapter.

{{learner-a}} copies a ready-made reference from the library's discovery service and pastes it in, then copies another from a PDF for the next source. The two are laid out differently - one puts the date in brackets, the other does not - and {{learner-a}} does not notice. The parts are all there somewhere, but the list mixes styles and no single pattern holds.

{{learner-b}} builds each reference from its parts: author's surname and initial first, then the date, the title (with the book title in italics), and the publication details, all in the one style the department asks for. Because {{learner-b}} can see the parts, every reference follows the same pattern and a reader can scan the list with confidence.

Both students had the same sources. Only {{learner-b}} recognised the parts and the style, and produced a reference list that holds together.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students use an author's idea, in their own words, in an essay.

{{learner-a}} rewrites the author's point as a neat sentence of their own and moves on, giving no reference because nothing has been quoted directly. The sentence reads as {{learner-a}}'s own thinking. But the idea is the author's, and with no reference it is now presented as {{learner-a}}'s - the very thing referencing exists to prevent.

{{learner-b}} also puts the author's point into their own words, but adds an in-text reference to the author and date. When {{learner-b}} does quote directly, the exact words go in quotation marks with a page number. Quote or paraphrase, the idea is credited to the author either way.

Both students paraphrased accurately. Only {{learner-b}} recognised that a paraphrase needs a reference just as a quotation does.

title: Referencing habits
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These habits turn referencing from a chore into something that works for you. Try them on your next piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I recorded where each idea came from as I used it, not just at the end?
Have I credited the author whenever I used their idea, theory or finding?
Can a reader tell which ideas are mine and which I have borrowed?
Does my reference list show the range of reading behind my work?
Am I referencing to credit and evidence, rather than only to avoid plagiarism?

title: Reading a reference
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these questions to read any reference and to check your own. Try them on a reference in your subject.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Can I find the author (surname first, then initial)?
Can I find the date the work was published?
Can I find the title, and is a book title set in italics?
Can I find where the work was published or found?
Do I know which style my department asks me to use?
Does the reference follow that one style consistently?

title: Referencing accurately
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves keep your referencing accurate. Try them the next time you use a source.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I added a reference wherever I used someone else's idea?
Have I referenced my paraphrases, not just my direct quotes?
Are my quotations in quotation marks, with a page number?
Did I build the reference from its parts rather than pasting one in?
Have I used one style consistently throughout?
Have I checked the author, date and title in each reference?

displayTitle: While writing in {{context}}, you put an author's finding into your own words. Which is the accurate way to reference it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the accurate way to reference a paraphrase?

_items.text: Add an in-text reference to the author and date, even though you did not quote.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a paraphrase needs a reference just as a quotation does.

_items.text: Leave it unreferenced, because you did not use the exact words.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase uses the author's idea, so it still needs a reference.

_items.text: Put the whole paraphrase in quotation marks.
_items.feedback: Quotation marks are for exact words; a paraphrase is referenced, not quoted.

_items.text: Reference it only if someone asks where the idea came from.
_items.feedback: You reference as you write, not only when challenged.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a paraphrase takes an in-text reference to the author and date.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Remember that a paraphrase still uses the author's idea.
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, a paraphrase takes an in-text reference to the author and date. You do not leave it unreferenced, quote it, or wait to be asked.

body: What does it mean to reference a source?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to reference a source?

_items.text: To acknowledge where an idea, finding or wording in your work came from.
_items.feedback: Yes. Referencing credits the source of what you have used.

_items.text: To summarise everything the source says.
_items.feedback: A summary is not a reference; a reference acknowledges the source.

_items.text: To add length to your essay.
_items.feedback: Referencing is about crediting sources, not length.

_items.text: To list every book on the subject.
_items.feedback: You reference the sources you used, not everything that exists.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Referencing acknowledges where what you used came from.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reference records.

body: Which of these is a reason references matter beyond avoiding plagiarism?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a reason references matter beyond avoiding plagiarism?

_items.text: They show a tutor the scope and quality of your reading.
_items.feedback: Yes. A reference list evidences the research behind your work.

_items.text: They make the essay harder to read.
_items.feedback: That is not a purpose of referencing.

_items.text: They replace the need to write an argument.
_items.feedback: References support an argument; they do not replace it.

_items.text: They guarantee a high mark on their own.
_items.feedback: References support your work but do not guarantee a mark by themselves.

_feedback.correct: That's right. References show the reading behind your work and help evidence it against the criteria.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reference list signals to a reader.

body: Which statement about referencing styles is correct?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement about referencing styles is correct?

_items.text: Different disciplines use different styles, such as Harvard, APA or Vancouver.
_items.feedback: Yes. The style depends on the discipline, and your department sets it.

_items.text: Every subject uses exactly the same style.
_items.feedback: Styles differ by discipline.

_items.text: You may change style freely within one piece of work.
_items.feedback: You keep to one style consistently.

_items.text: Referencing styles only apply to quotations.
_items.feedback: Styles govern all references, including paraphrases and the list.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Disciplines use different styles, and you keep to the one your department sets.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whether every subject references the same way.

body: A reference gives the author, the date, the title and where the work was published. What are these?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: The author, date, title and publication details of a reference are...

_items.text: The parts every reference is built from.
_items.feedback: Yes. Whatever the style, a reference is built from these parts.

_items.text: Optional extras you can leave out.
_items.feedback: These are the core parts of a reference, not optional.

_items.text: Details that only matter in Harvard style.
_items.feedback: Every style records these parts, formatted its own way.

_items.text: The same thing as an in-text citation.
_items.feedback: The in-text reference is brief; these are the full details in the list.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Author, date, title and publication details are the parts of a reference.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what every reference needs to contain.

body: When do you need an in-text reference?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: When do you need an in-text reference?

_items.text: Both when you quote and when you paraphrase.
_items.feedback: Yes. A paraphrase uses the author's idea, so it needs a reference too.

_items.text: Only when you quote exact words.
_items.feedback: Paraphrases need references as well.

_items.text: Only in the reference list at the end.
_items.feedback: You need in-text references as well as the list.

_items.text: Only when you are unsure of your point.
_items.feedback: You reference whenever you use someone else's idea.

_feedback.correct: That's right. You reference both quotations and paraphrases.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Remember a paraphrase still uses the author's idea.

body: A student puts an author's idea into their own words but gives no reference. What is the problem?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student paraphrases an author's idea with no reference. What is the problem?

_items.text: The author's idea is now presented as the student's own.
_items.feedback: Yes. An unreferenced paraphrase takes credit for a borrowed idea.

_items.text: It is fine, because the words are the student's own.
_items.feedback: The words are the student's, but the idea is the author's and must be credited.

_items.text: The paraphrase is too accurate.
_items.feedback: Accuracy is not the problem; the missing reference is.

_items.text: Paraphrasing is not allowed at university.
_items.feedback: Paraphrasing is fine; it just needs a reference.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Without a reference, a paraphrase presents the author's idea as the student's own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whose idea it is, even in the student's words.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what referencing is and why it matters, the styles and the parts a reference is built from, and how to reference accurately when you quote and paraphrase. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one habit you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to reference like an expert. The aim is to see these three ideas as one habit you use each time, rather than three separate things, so it carries on past this course and into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how what referencing is, the parts of a reference, and referencing accurately connect as one habit
show the whole referencing habit at work in a worked example of how a student handles a source
plan one way you will use the three together on your next piece of {{context}} work

title: Concept: definition
body: Referencing is one habit, not three separate skills. Every time you use a source, the same three things work together. You know why you are crediting it, you know the parts a reference is made of, and you set it out accurately. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are parts of one habit, and you use them together each time you draw on a source.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this means using the same habit on every source, in any subject. You credit the idea, build the reference from its parts in your style, and check it is accurate, in that order. A single ready-made reference pasted in at the end rarely holds up as well. Over a term, making this your normal way of working is what keeps your referencing trustworthy.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the next piece of work you have coming up. How will you use the whole referencing habit on it, from crediting an idea to checking the reference is accurate?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Referencing is most useful when you treat it as one habit, not three separate ideas. Each time you use a source you run the same strands together: know why you credit it, know its parts, and set it out accurately. Making this your normal way of working, source after source, is what keeps your referencing trustworthy.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Referencing is one habit you run each time you use a source, not three separate skills. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Notice
_items.body: Notice that you are using someone else's idea, whether you quote it directly or put it in your own words.

_items.title: Remember why
_items.body: Remember why you reference - to credit the idea and to show the reading behind your work.

_items.title: Build the reference
_items.body: Build the reference from its parts - author, date, title and publication details - in your department's style.

_items.title: Check
_items.body: Check the reference is accurate and consistent before you hand the work in - the next source then starts the habit again.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students each use several sources in the same essay. Student A pastes in ready-made references at the end and references only the quotations, missing the paraphrases. Student B uses the whole habit instead: crediting each idea, building each reference from its parts in one style, and checking them for accuracy. Both had the same sources, but Student B's referencing is trustworthy, because every strand was used together.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to use the one referencing habit
body: Use these to check you are using the whole habit, not just part of it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I notice that I was using someone else's idea, whether I quoted or paraphrased it?
Did I remember why I reference, rather than treating it as a chore at the end?
Did I build the reference from its parts in one consistent style?
Did I check the reference for errors instead of pasting in a ready-made one?
Will I use this same habit every time I use a source this term?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat referencing as one habit rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat referencing as one habit rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because the three work together every time you use a source: you know why you credit it, what a reference is made of, and how to set it out.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands act together each time, so referencing becomes one habit.

_items.text: Because knowing one of the three means you can skip the other two.
_items.feedback: No. The point is that the three work together, not that one replaces the others.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to think about the parts of a reference again.
_items.feedback: Not so. Knowing the parts is one of the three things the habit uses.

_items.text: Because one habit takes less effort than remembering why referencing matters.
_items.feedback: The gain is not less effort. It is that the three strands support one another.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Referencing is one habit whose three strands work together each time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the three strands work together when you use a source.

displayTitle: A student uses an author's idea in an essay. They put it in their own words, add an in-text reference, build it from its parts in their department's style, and check it is accurate. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student uses an author's idea in an essay. They put it in their own words, add an in-text reference, build it from its parts in their department's style, and check it is accurate. What does this show?

_items.text: That the student is using the whole referencing habit: knowing it is needed, building it from its parts, and setting it out accurately.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three strands are there, working together as one habit.

_items.text: That the student is doing more than referencing a source needs.
_items.feedback: No. Each part does a different job, and together they make the reference trustworthy.

_items.text: That only the in-text reference really matters.
_items.feedback: Not so. Crediting, the parts and accuracy all matter together.

_items.text: That paraphrasing does not need a reference.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase needs a reference just as a quotation does.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student used all three strands together as one habit.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Notice how the student uses all three strands at once.

displayTitle: You want to use this one referencing habit to handle sources well in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats referencing as one habit?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this one referencing habit to handle sources well in your subject this term. Which plan best treats referencing as one habit?

_items.text: Each time you use a source, credit the idea, build the reference from its parts in your style, and check it is accurate.
_items.feedback: Yes. That uses all three strands together, every time you use a source.

_items.text: Add all your references at the end, copied ready-made, without checking them.
_items.feedback: That drops the accuracy strand and treats referencing as a chore again.

_items.text: Only reference the sources you quote directly, and skip the ones you paraphrase.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase needs a reference too, so this leaves out part of the habit.

_items.text: Learn one referencing style and never check your references against it.
_items.feedback: Knowing the style only helps if you also check your references are accurate.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The whole habit, used each time, is what handles sources well.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that uses all three strands together.

_items.text: Credit each idea as it is used, build every reference from its parts in one style, and check them for accuracy.
